topics.title: HashMap Internals, Treeification & Concurrency Pitfalls
topics.summary: Deep dive into HashMap hashing, bucket index calculation, collision handling with Red-Black trees, and ConcurrentHashMap lock striping.
topics.content:
## HashMap Internals & Memory Architecture

### Bucket Array & Hash Calculation
HashMap uses an array of `Node<K,V>` buckets with default initial capacity `16` and load factor `0.75`.

```java
// 1. Bit-shift hash calculation to spread high bits to low bits:
static final int hash(Object key) {
    int h;
    return (key == null) ? 0 : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
}

// 2. Fast modulo via bitwise AND (Capacity must always be a power of 2!):
int index = (n - 1) & hash;
```

### Java 8 Treeification Mechanism
In Java 7, collisions formed a linked list with $O(n)$ search time. Java 8 converts a bucket to a **Red-Black Tree** ($O(\log n)$ search) when:
1. The bucket length reaches **`TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8`**.
2. Total table capacity is at least **`MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64`** (otherwise, it simply resizes the array).
3. If elements decrease to **`UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6`**, it converts back to a linked list.

```
Bucket Collision Progression:
Linked List (< 8 elements)      Red-Black Tree (>= 8 elements)
[Head] ──► [Node] ──► [Node]       ┌───[Root]───┐
                                  /              \
                            [Left Child]    [Right Child]
```

### Why ConcurrentHashMap Replaces Hashtable
- **Hashtable / Collections.synchronizedMap**: Locks the **entire map** for every operation using a single monitor lock. All threads queue up.
- **ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8+)**: Uses fine-grained **Node-level locking (`synchronized` on the bucket head node)** and CAS (Compare-And-Swap) for empty bucket insertions. Different threads write to different buckets simultaneously with zero blocking!
topics.interviewTip: Explain why table size is strictly a power of 2: Because '(n - 1) & hash' is equivalent to 'hash % n' only when n is 2^k, and bitwise AND is exponentially faster than division.

topics.title: Java 21 Virtual Threads (Project Loom) & Carrier Thread Scheduling
topics.summary: How Virtual Threads decouple thread creation from OS threads, unmounting during blocking I/O to achieve massive concurrency.
topics.content:
## Java 21 Virtual Threads (Project Loom)

### Platform Threads vs Virtual Threads

| Attribute | Platform (OS) Thread | Virtual Thread (Java 21) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Mapping** | 1:1 with OS Kernel Thread | $M:N$ (Millions of virtual threads onto few carrier threads) |
| **Memory Stack** | ~1MB fixed OS stack | Starts at ~few hundred bytes in JVM heap, grows dynamically |
| **Creation Cost** | Expensive (system call to OS) | Negligible (cheap Java heap object) |
| **Context Switch** | Slow (kernel trap / CPU register swap) | Fast (user-space JVM continuation unmount) |

### The Continuation Mechanism (Mounting & Unmounting)
When code inside a Virtual Thread calls a blocking operation (`SocketChannel.read()`, `Thread.sleep()`, JDBC query):
1. The underlying standard library detects the block.
2. The Virtual Thread **unmounts** from its Carrier Thread (ForkJoinPool worker).
3. The Carrier Thread is immediately free to run other Virtual Threads.
4. When I/O completes, the OS notifies the JVM (via epoll/kqueue), and the Virtual Thread is **mounted back** onto any available Carrier Thread.

```
100,000 Virtual Threads ──► [JVM Scheduler] ──► 8 Carrier OS Threads (CPU Cores)
```

### Pinning Trap: What to Avoid
A Virtual Thread becomes **pinned** to its carrier thread (cannot unmount) if it blocks inside:
1. A `synchronized` block/method (Replace with `ReentrantLock`!).
2. A native JNI method call.
topics.interviewTip: Emphasize that Virtual Threads are intended for high-throughput I/O-bound microservices, NOT CPU-intensive tasks (where carrier threads would remain fully occupied).

topics.title: ThreadPoolExecutor Architecture, Rejection Policies & Tuning
topics.summary: Master ThreadPoolExecutor sizing formulas, core vs max pool dynamics, bounded vs unbounded queues, and rejection policies.
topics.content:
## ThreadPoolExecutor Deep Dive

### Core Execution Flow
When a new task is submitted via `execute(Runnable)`:
1. If `activeThreads < corePoolSize`: Create a new worker thread to run the task immediately.
2. If `activeThreads >= corePoolSize`: Attempt to enqueue the task into the **WorkQueue**.
3. If queue is full AND `activeThreads < maxPoolSize`: Spawn a new non-core thread to run the task.
4. If queue is full AND `activeThreads >= maxPoolSize`: Invoke the **RejectedExecutionHandler**!

```
Task Submitted 
      │
      ▼
active < corePoolSize? ──(Yes)──► Create Core Thread
      │ (No)
      ▼
Enqueue into WorkQueue? ──(Yes)──► Queued for Worker
      │ (No, Queue Full!)
      ▼
active < maxPoolSize? ──(Yes)──► Create Non-Core Thread
      │ (No, Pool Full!)
      ▼
Invoke Rejection Policy (Abort / CallerRuns / Discard)
```

### Production Configuration Example
```java
ThreadPoolExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    10,                                  // corePoolSize
    50,                                  // maximumPoolSize
    60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,               // keepAliveTime for idle non-core threads
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500),       // Bounded queue (Never use unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue in prod!)
    new NamedThreadFactory("order-worker-"),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // Throttles producer by running task on calling thread
);
```

### Thread Pool Sizing Formulas
- **CPU-Bound Tasks**: $\text{Threads} = \text{CPU Cores} + 1$ (minimizes context switching).
- **I/O-Bound Tasks**: $\text{Threads} = \text{CPU Cores} \times \left(1 + \frac{\text{Wait Time}}{\text{Compute Time}}\right)$

references.title: Brian Goetz: Java Concurrency in Practice

topics.interviewTip: Never use Executors.newFixedThreadPool() or newCachedThreadPool() in production! newFixed uses an unbounded queue (OOM risk) and newCached spawns Integer.MAX_VALUE threads (CPU thrashing).

topics.title: JVM Memory Model: Stack vs Heap, Metaspace & GC (G1 vs ZGC)
topics.summary: Understand JVM memory spaces, object headers, garbage collection pauses, G1 GC regions, and ZGC sub-millisecond pauses.
topics.content:
## JVM Memory Model & Modern Garbage Collectors

### Memory Areas
- **Heap**: Shared across threads. Stores all class instances and arrays. Divided into Young Gen (Eden, S0, S1) and Old Gen.
- **Stack**: Private per thread. Stores primitive local variables and references to heap objects in Stack Frames.
- **Metaspace**: Off-heap native memory. Stores class metadata, bytecode, method structures (replaced PermGen in Java 8).

```
JVM Memory Layout:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Heap (Shared, GC-Managed)                              │
│ ┌─────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────┐ │
│ │ Young Gen (Eden, S0, S1)│  │ Old Generation (Tenured)│
│ └─────────────────────────┘  └───────────────────────┘ │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Native Memory (Off-Heap)                               │
│ ├── Metaspace (Class Metadata)                         │
│ ├── Thread Stacks (1MB per thread)                     │
│ └── Direct Byte Buffers (Netty zero-copy I/O)         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### G1 GC vs ZGC Comparison

| Feature | G1 GC (Default Java 9+) | ZGC (Production Java 17+) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Architecture** | Memory divided into ~2,048 equal regions (1MB to 32MB) | Region-based, colored pointers, load barriers |
| **Pause Times** | 50ms - 200ms (Soft goal tunable via `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`) | **Sub-millisecond (< 1ms)** regardless of heap size! |
| **Max Heap Size** | Up to ~64GB | **Terabytes (up to 16TB)** with zero pause increase |
| **Compaction** | Incremental evacuation pause | Concurrent compaction while Java threads run |

### Debugging OutOfMemoryError (OOM)
- `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`: Memory leak (e.g., static collections, unclosed ThreadLocal, connection leaks).
- `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`: Too many dynamically generated classes (CGLIB, classloader leak).
- **Diagnostics**: Analyze heap dumps using Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT) via `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`.

references.title: Oracle JVM Garbage Collection Tuning Guide

topics.interviewTip: Explain colored pointers and load barriers in ZGC: ZGC stores reference state in pointer metadata bits and intercepts references on the fly to perform concurrent evacuation.

topics.title: Spring Boot Auto-Configuration & Bean Lifecycle Hooks
topics.summary: How Spring Boot auto-configures beans via @Conditional annotations and standard ApplicationContext lifecycle hooks.
topics.content:
## Spring Boot Auto-Configuration & IoC Container

### Auto-Configuration Under the Hood
When `@SpringBootApplication` starts:
1. `@EnableAutoConfiguration` reads configuration class names from:
   `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`.
2. Each auto-configuration class is evaluated against conditional annotations:
   - `@ConditionalOnClass`: Applies only if specific JAR classes are in classpath (e.g. `KafkaTemplate.class`).
   - `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`: Backs off if the developer already declared their own `@Bean`.
   - `@ConditionalOnProperty`: Evaluates `application.yml` flags.

```java
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)
@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "spring.datasource", name = "url")
public class DataSourceAutoConfiguration {
    
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    public DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties properties) {
        return properties.initializeDataSourceBuilder().build();
    }
}
```

### Spring Bean Lifecycle Phases

```
1. BeanDefinition Loading
2. Instantiation (Constructor call)
3. Dependency Injection (Field/Setter/Constructor injection)
4. BeanNameAware / ApplicationContextAware callbacks
5. BeanPostProcessor: postProcessBeforeInitialization
6. @PostConstruct / InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()
7. Custom init-method
8. BeanPostProcessor: postProcessAfterInitialization (AOP Proxies created here!)
9. Ready for Service
10. @PreDestroy / DisposableBean.destroy() on context shutdown
```

### Why Constructor Injection is Mandatory
- Makes dependencies `final` (immutable thread safety).
- Prevents `NullPointerException` during unit tests without needing Spring reflection.
- Detects circular dependencies immediately during startup.
topics.interviewTip: Point out that Spring AOP proxies (like @Transactional and @Async) are created in the BeanPostProcessor afterInitialization phase.
